title: Builders and ported tests

story: You pick the first integration test to move off shared QA and into the new API layer: a permission test that checks what a collaborating workgroup may do in a project. It is short and it never needs an on-prem client, so it should be easy. Then you read its first lines. The collaborator is a workgroup with a fixed ID, 65e46694-0951-4634-a839-634af42a8177, which someone created by hand on QA years ago. In the new layer every run starts from an empty, freshly migrated database, and that workgroup does not exist.

The quick fix is a few lines of factory code that write a workgroup row straight into the database. It would make the test green, but it would also skip everything the product does when a workgroup is really created: the serializer's checks, the permissions and the rows that come with it. The test would then check the API's rules against data that the API itself could never have made.
hook.question: How does a test in the new layer get the users, workgroups and projects it needs, made the way the product makes them, without any fixed IDs from QA?

read.h: A shared environment remembers every run
p: Tests on QA lean on what QA already contains: a workgroup created by hand, a user with a known password, an offline client with an ID like cafecafe-…-000000000004. That works as long as nobody deletes those rows and nobody else's test changes them. QA also keeps whatever each run created, so the second run of a test starts in a different world than the first. You will see it in the lab: the same script against the same server answers 201 the first time and 500 the second, because the user it creates already exists, and the project list grows by one on every run.

The API layer gives each test a fresh database, so a test can no longer find its world; it has to build it. That rule, every test builds what it needs and nothing is shared, also makes the tests independent of each other and of the order they run in, which pytest-xdist needs anyway.

$ uv run python qa_style.py     # the same script again

read.h: Builders go through the front door
p: There are two ways to create test data. A factory, for example with the factory_boy library, writes rows straight into the database: fast and simple, and fine for a unit test of one model. But it skips the serializer, the permission checks and every field the API fills in by itself. In the lab, the API sets a project's workgroup and creator from the logged-in user, so a project written by a factory has no creator, and the database refuses it; give it one by hand and the factory happily stores a project with a blank name, which the API would refuse with 400.

A builder creates the same data through the API, the way the UI and the SDK do. It is a small function with a clear name, such as builder.site() or builder.project(site), that calls the real endpoints, fills every value the test does not care about with fake data from the Faker library, and returns what the test needs, usually IDs and a logged-in client. The data then exists only because the API agreed to create it. In fcp, builder.site() posts to the test-data endpoint the cloud already has for QA and returns a fresh workgroup with its own user; only the first Rhino admin that bootstraps everything comes from a factory.

read.h: The same calls, a different transport
p: fcp's integration tests already have a client for the API: a class, RhinoAPI, that logs in, sends each request with the requests library and raises a clear error on a bad status, plus a wrapper with one method per action, such as create_project(). Ported tests should keep those calls, so the only thing that changes is how a request travels. The trick is a seam inside the client. All its network traffic goes through one method, _send, and a subclass for the API layer overrides only that method: instead of an HTTP request to QA, it hands the same method, URL, headers and body to DRF's APIClient, which runs them inside the test process.

Everything else in the client stays real, including the login. The in-process client gets its token from the real token endpoint with the user's real password, so authentication is tested on every call, and the wrapper's error handling works as before. In fcp, the first change is to move the two requests.request(...) calls in the integration tests' client into one _send method, which changes nothing for the runs against QA, and only then to add the in-process subclass.

notes.text: A subclass of the client the QA tests use, so every method they call still exists.
A path instead of a host: requests stay inside Django.
The only override. RhinoAPI calls _send for the login and for every request.
Django's test client reads headers as META keys: Authorization becomes HTTP_AUTHORIZATION.

read.h: Porting a test: move it, don't copy it
p: With builders and the in-process client, a ported test reads almost like the original. Its own calls stay, and each fixed ID from QA becomes a builder call, so the collaborating workgroup from the story becomes a fresh builder.site(). The test asserts on what a caller sees, the status code, the error text, the fields and the number of rows, and never on which internal functions ran, so it survives a refactoring.

Moving is a process, not a copy. The original stays on QA for a while, marked to run only in the nightly run, and is deleted once the port has been green in CI for two weeks. Not every test can move: a test that needs a real indexing machine or a search cluster stays on QA, and a port may check that the work was queued without running it.

code.text:
"""Ported from the QA suite. There, the other site was a hard-coded workgroup that had to exist on QA:
OTHER_WORKGROUP = "65e46694-0951-4634-a839-634af42a8177". Here each test builds its own sites."""


def test_a_site_sees_only_its_own_projects(builder):
    mine, other = builder.site(), builder.site()
    mine.api.create_project("Lung CT")
    assert [p["name"] for p in mine.api.list_projects()] == ["Lung CT"]
    assert other.api.list_projects() == []


def test_the_api_records_who_created_a_project(builder):
    site = builder.site()
    site.api.create_project("Lung CT")
    [project] = site.api.list_projects()
    assert (project["workgroup"], project["created_by"]) == (site.workgroup, site.email)

notes.text: Two fresh sites instead of one site plus a fixed workgroup from QA.
The other site sees nothing: the API's own filtering, checked from the outside.

deeper.h: Go deeper: datasets need the fake client
p: Most real scenarios need more than a project: a data schema, a dataset and a code object. A dataset is imported by the site's on-prem client, so its builder uses the fake from the previous lesson. It creates the dataset through POST datasets/ like the UI, finds the import task the fake recorded, and calls complete_task with a successful status and fake rows made with Faker, which runs the cloud's real response handler. Then it checks through the API that the import finished.

One detail matters: the import must be started asynchronously. A synchronous import makes the request wait in the test's own thread for the client's answer, and since the test is the one that delivers the answer, it would wait forever. So the wrapper's create_dataset gets a sync parameter that the builder sets to false.

lab.title: Builders through the API, and one client for HTTP and in-process
needs: Two terminal tabs (one runs a server for a few minutes)
lab.goal: See how a shared server remembers every run, then make tests build their own sites through the API, using the same client class in-process instead of over HTTP.

guess.q: A builder creates a project by writing Project.objects.create(name=..., workgroup=...) straight into the database. The API normally sets created_by from the logged-in user. What happens in a test that uses it?

options.text: It works, because the database fills created_by in by itself.
options.why: Nothing fills it. It is the API's perform_create that sets the creator, and a factory never runs it.

options.text: The insert fails with NOT NULL constraint failed on created_by, because the factory skipped the code that sets it.
options.why: The row is missing everything the API would add. Here the database notices; for a check that lives only in the serializer, nothing would.

options.text: The API refuses the request with 400.
options.why: There is no request. That is the point: the factory never goes through the API.

from django.conf import settings
from django.db import models


class Member(models.Model):
    user = models.OneToOneField(settings.AUTH_USER_MODEL, on_delete=models.CASCADE)
    workgroup = models.CharField(max_length=60)


class Project(models.Model):

cat > projects/views.py <<'EOF'
from django.contrib.auth.models import User
from rest_framework import serializers, status, viewsets
from rest_framework.permissions import AllowAny
from rest_framework.response import Response
from rest_framework.views import APIView

from .models import Member, Project


class ProjectSerializer(serializers.ModelSerializer):
    created_by = serializers.SlugRelatedField(slug_field="email", read_only=True)

    class Meta:
        model = Project
        fields = ["id", "name", "workgroup", "created_by"]
        read_only_fields = ["workgroup"]


class ProjectViewSet(viewsets.ModelViewSet):
    serializer_class = ProjectSerializer

    def get_queryset(self):
        return Project.objects.filter(workgroup=self.request.user.member.workgroup).order_by("id")

    def perform_create(self, serializer):  # the API decides the workgroup and the creator, never the caller
        serializer.save(workgroup=self.request.user.member.workgroup, created_by=self.request.user)


class SiteSerializer(serializers.Serializer):
    workgroup = serializers.SlugField()
    email = serializers.EmailField()
    password = serializers.CharField(min_length=12)


class TestSiteView(APIView):
    """Test data only: a workgroup and its first user, like fcp's test-data endpoint."""

    permission_classes = [AllowAny]

    def post(self, request):
        site = SiteSerializer(data=request.data)
        site.is_valid(raise_exception=True)
        email, workgroup = site.validated_data["email"], site.validated_data["workgroup"]
        user = User.objects.create_user(username=email, email=email, password=site.validated_data["password"])
        Member.objects.create(user=user, workgroup=workgroup)
        return Response({"workgroup": workgroup, "email": email}, status=status.HTTP_201_CREATED)
EOF
cat > mysite/urls.py <<'EOF'
from django.urls import path
from rest_framework.authtoken.views import obtain_auth_token
from rest_framework.routers import DefaultRouter

from projects.views import ProjectViewSet, TestSiteView

router = DefaultRouter()
router.register("api/projects", ProjectViewSet, basename="project")
urlpatterns = [
    path("api/token/", obtain_auth_token),
    path("api/test-data/site/", TestSiteView.as_view()),
    *router.urls,
]
EOF

"""The same RhinoAPI, with the network swapped for DRF's APIClient: same calls, same login, no server."""
import json

from rest_framework.test import APIClient

from api import RhinoAPI


class InProcessAPI(RhinoAPI):
    def __init__(self, email: str, password: str):
        super().__init__("/api/", email, password)
        self.client = APIClient()

    def _send(self, method, url, headers, json_body):
        meta = {"HTTP_" + name.upper().replace("-", "_"): value for name, value in headers.items()}
        body = json.dumps(json_body) if json_body is not None else ""
        return self.client.generic(method, url, body, content_type="application/json", **meta)
EOF
cat > tests/conftest.py <<'EOF'
from dataclasses import dataclass

import pytest
from faker import Faker
from rest_framework.test import APIClient

from inprocess import InProcessAPI

fake = Faker()


@dataclass
class Site:
    api: InProcessAPI  # logged in as the site's first user
    workgroup: str
    email: str


class Builder:
    def site(self) -> Site:
        """A fresh workgroup and user, made through the API's test-data endpoint. Fake data only."""
        workgroup, email, password = f"wg-{fake.unique.slug()}", fake.unique.email(), fake.password(length=16)
        response = APIClient().post("/api/test-data/site/", {"workgroup": workgroup, "email": email, "password": password}, format="json")
        assert response.status_code == 201, response.json()
        return Site(InProcessAPI(email, password), workgroup, email)


@pytest.fixture
def builder(db):
    return Builder()
EOF

lab.build: Add a project builder and port two more tests. In tests/conftest.py, give Builder a method project(site, name=None) that creates the project through site.api.create_project, with a Faker catch_phrase when no name is given, and returns the ID. Then write tests/test_project_access.py with two tests: another site that asks for GET projects/<id>/ of my project gets an ApiError with 404, and a project named " " (a single space) is refused with an ApiError with 400. Use pytest.raises(ApiError, match="404") and match="400".
checks: uv run pytest -q prints 4 passed, and passes again on a second run.
No test file contains a fixed workgroup, email or ID: every site comes from builder.site().
builder.project calls the API (create_project), not Project.objects.
The 404 test proves the other site cannot even see that the project exists.
The blank-name test fails if you make builder.project write the row directly (see Fix it).

solution.text:
# tests/conftest.py, inside class Builder
    def project(self, site: Site, name: str | None = None) -> int:
        """A project made by the site's own user, through POST projects/."""
        return site.api.create_project(name or fake.catch_phrase())


# tests/test_project_access.py
import pytest

from api import ApiError


def test_another_site_cannot_open_my_project(builder):
    mine, other = builder.site(), builder.site()
    project_id = builder.project(mine)
    with pytest.raises(ApiError, match="404"):
        other.api.make_call("GET", f"projects/{project_id}/")


def test_a_project_needs_a_name(builder):
    with pytest.raises(ApiError, match="400"):
        builder.project(builder.site(), name=" ")

lab.done: Four tests pass in-process with no fixed IDs, and you can say why the builder goes through the API instead of writing rows.

check.q: A ported test needs a second workgroup. On QA it used a fixed ID created by hand years ago. What should the ported test do?

options.text: Insert a workgroup row with that same fixed ID in a fixture, so the rest of the test stays unchanged.
options.why: It keeps the test tied to a made-up ID and skips everything the product does when a workgroup is created.

options.text: Call builder.site() and use the workgroup it returns.
options.why: A fresh site made through the API: no shared state, no fixed ID, and the creation path is tested too.

options.text: Stay on QA, because the API layer cannot have two workgroups.
options.why: It can have as many as the test builds. A test only needs QA when it needs a real client or real infrastructure.

check.q: Why do builders create data through the API instead of with factories that write rows?

options.text: Because API calls are faster than database inserts.
options.why: They are slower. We pay a little speed for data that the product could really contain.

options.text: Because factories cannot create related rows.
options.why: factory_boy handles related rows well. The issue is what factories skip, not what they can build.

options.text: Because the API runs the serializer, the permission checks and the fields it fills in itself, so tests only ever see data the product could really create.
options.why: A test that starts from impossible data can pass while the real flow fails.

check.q: The in-process client overrides only _send. What does that buy a ported test?

options.text: Its calls, such as create_project(), stay exactly as they were, and the login, error handling and pagination remain the real client's code.
options.why: Only the transport changes. Everything a QA test relied on still runs.

options.text: It no longer needs to log in, which makes it faster.
options.why: It still logs in through the real token endpoint with a real password; that is a feature, not a cost.

options.text: It can now reach QA and the test database at the same time.
options.why: It talks only to Django inside the test process. QA is not involved at all.

p: In rhinoCore/integration-tests/integration_test_utils/common.py, RhinoAPI.make_call (including its page fetches) moves its requests.request calls into one _send() method. tests_api/api.py adds InProcessRhinoAPI, which overrides _send and _request_jwt_token with DRF's APIClient and still gets a real JWT from auth/obtain_token. tests_api/builders.py adds the builder fixture: builder.site() posts test/create_test_data with TestDataCreator's custom scenario, builder.project(), data_schema() with the CSVs in pytest_fixtures/, dataset() with sync=False and FakeOnPremClient.complete_task, code_object() and the pneumonia and python_code scenario helpers. api_client keeps the name of the integration fixture, so ported tests run almost unchanged.

The first port moves 8 cloud-only tests (permission/test_project_permission.py, test_client_offline_validation.py, a TensorBoard test and a runtime-file test), replacing the QA IDs 65e46694-… and cafecafe-…-000000000004 with builders and the fake's offline_agents. The second moves the six custom-vocabulary tests and the large vocabulary upload, which checks that the indexing chain was queued in the task-queue fake without draining it; the very large upload and the full indexing flow stay on the QA nightly. Originals get @pytest.mark.nightly and are deleted after two green weeks. Known gap: the vocabulary sketch calls upload_large_vocabulary, which does not exist in fcp.

tickets.why: The _send seam, InProcessRhinoAPI, builder.site(), builder.project() and the api_client fixture.
Builders for schemas, datasets (through the fake client) and code objects, plus the scenario helpers.
Port the first 8 cloud-only integration tests: move, don't copy.
Port the 7 vocabulary tests, bringing the total to 15.

words.plain: A small test helper that creates data through the API and returns what the test needs, such as IDs and a logged-in client.
A helper (for example factory_boy) that writes rows straight into the database, skipping the API.
How a request travels: over HTTP to a server, or in-process through Django's test client.
Moving a test from QA to the API layer: same calls, builders instead of fixed IDs, then deleting the original.
A library that makes realistic fake names, emails and phrases, so tests never use real data.

review.q: List three things a QA test may rely on that a test in the API layer must build itself.
review.a: Workgroups or users created by hand with fixed IDs, known passwords, and rows left over from earlier runs (or a pre-seeded offline client).

review.q: Sketch the in-process client from memory: what does it subclass, what does it override, and how does a header reach Django?
review.a: It subclasses the QA client (RhinoAPI), overrides only _send, and passes headers as META keys, for example Authorization as HTTP_AUTHORIZATION, to APIClient.generic.

review.q: What are the steps for moving a QA test to the API layer?
review.a: Copy its calls, replace fixed IDs with builders, assert on what the caller sees, mark the QA original nightly, and delete it after two green weeks in CI.

remember: Let every test build its own world through the API's front door, and swap only the transport so ported tests keep their calls.
